q: 131. Bleeder wells are required to .............
explain: Bleeder wells relieve excess pore water pressure trapped beneath impervious layers, preventing uplift or blowout.

q: 132. Neutral stress refers to .............
explain: Neutral stress is another term for pore water pressure, the stress carried by water in the soil voids.

q: 133. The difference between total pressure and pore water pressure is known as .............
explain: Effective stress = total stress - pore water pressure, per Terzaghi's principle of effective stress.

q: 134. A flownet may be used for the determination of .............
explain: A flow net simultaneously provides exit gradient, seepage discharge, and seepage/uplift pressure at any point.

q: 135. Which of the following is responsible for shear resistance in soils?
options: Cohesion and adhesion between the soil particles
explain: Shear strength in soils arises from both inter-particle friction and cohesion/adhesion, combined in the Mohr-Coulomb equation.

q: 136. In an undrained plastic clay the shear strength is due to .............
explain: Under undrained conditions, saturated plastic clay exhibits an angle of friction close to zero, so its shear strength is governed by cohesion.

q: 137. Through a point in a loaded soil, the normal stress is maximum on .............
options: plane making an angle of 45 with principal planes
explain: By definition, principal planes carry zero shear, and the major principal plane carries the maximum normal stress.

q: 138. Darcy's law is applicable if a soil is .............
explain: Darcy's law assumptions require the soil to be homogeneous, incompressible, and isotropic for validity of the linear flow relation.

q: 139. According to Darcy's law, the flow velocity can be obtained by .............
explain: Darcy's law states discharge velocity v = Ki (permeability times hydraulic gradient).

q: 140. Coefficient of percolation has a value .............
options: less than the coefficient of permeability
equal to the coefficient of permeability
explain: Percolation velocity uses the effective (void) area rather than the gross area, making the coefficient of percolation greater than the coefficient of permeability.

q: 141. Stoke's law gives the following velocity of a spherical particle falling freely in an infinite liquid medium .............
explain: Stoke's Law describes the terminal (constant) settling velocity reached once gravitational and viscous drag forces balance.

q: 142. The depth of exploration for square footing should be at least .............
explain: For an isolated square footing, exploration should extend to about twice the footing width to capture the significant stressed zone.

q: 143. The depth of exploration of a strip footing should be at least .............
explain: For strip footings, exploration depth of about twice the footing width is recommended to capture the stress-influenced zone.

q: 144. The depth upto which the stress increment due to the applied loads can produce significant settlement is called as .............
explain: Significant depth is the term for the zone below a foundation where applied stress increments meaningfully contribute to settlement.

q: 145. The minimum depth of exploration in case of gravity dam is .............
explain: For gravity dams, exploration typically extends to a depth roughly equal to the height of the dam to characterize the stressed foundation zone.

q: 146. Stress distribution on the failure plane in the case of a triaxial test is .............
explain: In a properly conducted triaxial test, stresses are applied uniformly across the specimen's cross-section and failure plane.

q: 147. In unconfined compression test, around stress is .............
explain: The unconfined compression test applies no lateral (confining/cell) pressure, so the minor principal stress is zero.

q: 148. The expression for critical gradient is .............
explain: Critical hydraulic gradient is derived by equating upward seepage force to submerged weight: ic = (G-1)/(1+e).

q: 149. The presence of entrapped air in a soil will .............
explain: Entrapped air bubbles block pore channels, reducing the effective flow path and thus decreasing permeability.

q: 150. The value of coefficient of permeability of clays is .............
explain: Clays, with their very fine pores, have extremely low permeability, typically less than 10^-6 cm/s.

q: 151. Soils with a value for coefficient of permeability ranging between 10^-4 to 10^-6 are classified as .............
explain: This intermediate permeability range (10^-4 to 10^-6 cm/s) defines semi-pervious soils, such as silts.

q: 152. The workability of the following soil will be excellent as a construction material .............
explain: Well-graded gravel (GW) has excellent grading and drainage properties, making it an excellent construction material.

q: 153. A reduction of liquid limit after oven drying to a value less than three-fourth of the liquid limit before oven-drying is an indication of .............
explain: A significant drop in liquid limit after oven drying indicates loss of organic matter structure, a diagnostic test for organic soils.

q: 154. Soils which plot above the A-line, and which have a plasticity Index between 4 to 7 are classified as .............
explain: Soils in this narrow low-plasticity range near the A-line boundary are classified as CL-ML (dual classification).

q: 155. According to IS classification, the value of liquid limit for fine grained soils of high compressibility is .............
explain: IS classification uses LL = 50% as the boundary between low/intermediate and high compressibility fine-grained soils.

q: 156. The soil sample for the hydrometer analysis is pretreated with the following agent .............
explain: Hydrogen peroxide (an oxidising agent) is used to remove organic matter from the soil sample before hydrometer analysis.

q: 157. In a hydrometer analysis the reason for addition of hydrogen peroxide and heating it is to remove .............
explain: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes and removes organic matter, which would otherwise interfere with dispersion and settling of particles.

q: 158. In a hydrometer analysis for removing calcium compounds the following acid is used .............
explain: Dilute (0.2 N) hydrochloric acid is used to dissolve and remove calcium compounds before dispersion in hydrometer analysis.

q: 159. The compressibility of the following soil will be excellent when compacted and saturated .............
explain: Clayey gravel (GC) exhibits the highest compressibility among these coarse-grained classifications due to its clay fraction.

q: 160. According to IS code, the permissible values of total settlement in case of isolated footings on clayey and sands are .............
explain: IS 1904 permits total settlement of 65 mm for isolated footings on clay and 40 mm on sand.

q: 161. According to IS code, the permissible values of total settlements of rafts on clays and sands are .............
explain: For raft foundations, IS code permits larger total settlement: 100 mm on clay and 65 mm on sand.

q: 162. The type of settlement which causes more trouble for the stability of structure is .............
explain: Differential (uneven) settlement causes structural distortion and cracking, making it far more damaging than uniform settlement.
This is the standard formula for coefficient of curvature (Cc), used alongside Cu to assess grading.

q: 164. The symbol SP indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, SP denotes poorly graded sand.

q: 165. The symbol GM indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, GM denotes silty gravel.

q: 166. The symbol SC indicates .............
explain: In USCS notation, SC denotes clayey sand.

q: 167. Which of the following clays behave like a dense sand .............
options: over consolidated clay with a low OCR
over consolidated clay with a high OCR
explain: Heavily over-consolidated clay (high OCR) exhibits dilative, brittle behaviour similar to dense sand under shear.

q: 168. The damage will be severe if the angular distortion is about .............
explain: An angular distortion as large as 1/50 indicates severe structural distress based on standard settlement damage criteria.

q: 169. According to IS code, the permissible values of different settlements in case of clays and sands are .............
explain: IS code permits differential settlement of 40 mm on clay and 25 mm on sand for typical structures.

q: 170. There will be no damage for the structure if the angular distortion is about .............
explain: An angular distortion as small as 1/180 or less is generally considered safe, with no structural damage expected.

q: 171. The concept of useful width for the determination of bearing capacity is generally used for .............
explain: The 'useful width' (reduced effective width) concept accounts for load eccentricity, applying specifically to eccentrically loaded footings.

q: 172. The ratio of plasticity index to clay fraction is known as .............
explain: Activity of clay is defined as plasticity index divided by the percentage of clay-sized fraction (Skempton's activity).

q: 173. Rise in water table upto the ground surface results in .............
options: reduction of pore water pressure but no change in total stress
increase of pore water pressure and increase in total stress
increase of pore water pressure and increase in total stress
increase of pore water pressure and decrease in total stress
explain: As water table rises, both total stress (due to submerged unit weight change) and pore pressure increase together.

q: 174. The ratio of weight of water to the total weight of the soil is known as .............
explain: Water content is properly defined as the ratio of weight of water to the weight of solids, not total soil weight, so none of the given options is technically correct.

q: 175. The constant of proportionality between seepage velocity and hydraulic gradient is called .............
explain: Seepage (percolation) velocity relates to hydraulic gradient through the coefficient of percolation, which uses the net (void) cross-sectional area.

q: 176. Capillary force is dependent on .............
explain: Capillary rise and force in soil pores are governed primarily by the surface tension of water acting at the air-water meniscus.

q: 177. The zone of soil mass above the water table which is saturated by capillary moisture is called .............
explain: The capillary fringe is the zone directly above the water table kept saturated by capillary action.

q: 178. The number of heads that are used for defining the water head at a point in a soil mass are .............
explain: Total head at a point is composed of three components: elevation head, pressure head, and velocity head.

q: 179. Velocity head in soils will be .............
explain: Seepage velocities in soil are extremely small, making the velocity head component negligible compared to elevation and pressure heads.

q: 180. The pore water pressure in the capillary zone is .............
explain: Water held in the capillary fringe above the water table is under suction (tension), giving it negative pore water pressure.

q: 181. Water which the soil particles freely adsorb from atmosphere by the physical forces of attraction, and is held by the force of adhesion is known as .............
explain: Water adsorbed onto particle surfaces via physical attraction and adhesion can be described by any of these overlapping terms, so all apply.

q: 182. Capillary water is held in the interstices of soil due to capillarity forces. The capillary force depends upon .............
explain: Capillary force depends jointly on surface tension, water pressure, and the size of soil pores (which sets the meniscus curvature).

q: 183. Out of the following, which will have the maximum value of surface tension force .............
explain: Mercury has an exceptionally high surface tension compared to typical liquids like water, petrol, or acetone.

q: 184. A soil which does not permit the passage or seepage of any permeant through its voids, is known as .............
explain: A soil that blocks all seepage flow through its voids is, by definition, an impermeable soil.

q: 185. In most of the practical flow problems in soil mechanics, the flow is .............
explain: Given the very low seepage velocities in soils, flow is almost always laminar, satisfying the basis for Darcy's law.

q: 186. Which of the following soils will have least value of safe load?
explain: Soft chalk is the weakest and most compressible of these materials, giving it the lowest safe bearing load.

q: 187. Black cotton soil is not suitable for foundations because of its .............
explain: Black cotton soil contains montmorillonite, causing severe volumetric swelling and shrinkage with moisture changes, making it problematic for foundations.

q: 188. The soil transported by running water is called .............
explain: Soil transported and deposited by flowing rivers/streams is classified as alluvial soil.

q: 189. The soil transported by wind is called .............
explain: Wind-transported and deposited soil is termed aeolian soil (e.g., loess, dune sand).

q: 190. Westergaard's theory is more appropriate for .............
explain: Westergaard's stress distribution theory models soil with alternating rigid and elastic thin layers, making it suited to layered/stratified soil deposits.

q: 191. Generally hand augers are used when the depth is about .............
explain: Hand augers are a simple manual tool practical only for shallow exploration, typically up to about 6 m depth.

q: 192. The value of cohesion of a saturated clay will be ............. times the value of unconfined compression strength
explain: For saturated clay under undrained conditions, cohesion c = qu/2, i.e. half the unconfined compressive strength.

q: 193. Lacustrine soils are those soils which are .............
options: deposited at the bottom of the lakes
explain: Lacustrine soils are, by definition, transported by water and deposited at the bottom of lakes.

q: 194. Glacial soils are those soils which are .............
options: deposited at the bottom of the lakes
explain: Glacial soils are transported and deposited directly by glacier ice, which none of the given options describe.

q: 195. A critical hydraulic gradient occurs when .............
options: seepage pressure is in upward direction
explain: Critical gradient conditions require upward flow, upward seepage pressure equal to submerged weight, and consequently zero effective stress — all together.
